title: Create a gateway endpoint
content:
Open the Amazon VPC console In the navigation pane, choose Endpoints, then click Create Endpoint: You will see 6 existing VPC endpoints that support AWS Systems Manager (SSM). These endpoints were deployed automatically by the CloudFormation Templates for this workshop.
In the Create endpoint console: Specify name of the endpoint: s3-gwe In service category, choose AWS services In Services, type s3 in the search box and choose the service with type gateway For VPC, select VPC Cloud from the drop-down. For Configure route tables, select the route table that is already associated with two subnets (note: this is not the main route table for the VPC, but a second route table created by CloudFormation). For Policy, leave the default option, Full Access, to allow full access to the service. You will deploy a VPC endpoint policy in a later lab module to demonstrate restricting access to S3 buckets based on policies. Do not add a tag to the VPC endpoint at this time. title: Introduction
content:
VPC endpoints VPC endpoints are virtual devices. They are horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available VPC components. They allow communication between your compute resources and AWS services without imposing availability risks. Compute resources running in VPC can access Amazon S3 using a Gateway endpoint. PrivateLink interface endpoints can be used by compute resources running in VPC or on-premises. Workshop overview In this workshop, you will use two VPCs.
“VPC Cloud” is for cloud resources such as a Gateway endpoint and an EC2 instance to test with. “VPC On-Prem” simulates an on-premises environment such as a factory or corporate datacenter. An EC2 instance running strongSwan VPN software has been deployed in “VPC On-prem” and automatically configured to establish a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel with AWS Transit Gateway. This VPN simulates connectivity from an on-premises location to the AWS cloud. To minimize costs, only one VPN instance is provisioned to support this workshop. When planning VPN connectivity for your production workloads, AWS recommends using multiple VPN devices for high availability.

CI/CD on AWS: Integrating DevSecOps Before Production Deployment 1. Problem and objective Release speed matters little if new versions introduce security weaknesses. DevSecOps embeds risk checks into development so that problems can be addressed at the stage where they arise rather than only after deployment.
2. Designing an AWS pipeline Reference flow: Git → CodePipeline → CodeBuild → Staging → Security tests → Manual approval → Production.
Component Responsibility AWS CodePipeline Orchestrate release stages AWS CodeBuild Build, unit testing and scanner execution Amazon S3 Store pipeline artifacts AWS CodeDeploy Coordinate deployment on compatible platforms Amazon ECS Run container workloads in the reference architecture Amazon CloudWatch Monitor logs and execution results 3. Security checks Method Timing and purpose SCA Inspect dependencies for known vulnerabilities SAST Analyze source code without running the application DAST Test a running application in an authorized staging environment IAST Analyze an instrumented application during execution Define release-blocking criteria, such as unresolved critical findings. Retain scan reports for review. Scanners require separate configuration; CodePipeline does not perform every security test by itself.
4. Reference implementation workflow Connect the Git repository and configure the release branch. Create a build project and run unit tests, SCA and SAST. Fail the build when security policy is violated. Package the artifact and deploy the built revision to staging. Run DAST and IAST in a suitable test environment and collect findings. Add a manual approval gate before production. Deploy the tested artifact after approval. Monitor post-release errors and prepare a rollback to a stable revision. 5. Monitoring, permissions and risk control Use separate least-privilege IAM roles for pipeline stages and never store access keys in Git. Parameter Store or Secrets Manager can protect sensitive configuration. CloudTrail supports API activity auditing, AWS Config tracks resource configurations, and Security Hub consolidates findings from integrated sources.
Suggested validation cases include vulnerable dependencies, failed builds, unauthorized approvals and faulty staging releases. A pipeline should block unacceptable revisions instead of deploying them.
6. Connection to the internship project For Driver Drowsiness & Distraction Detection, pre-release checks can be applied to Lambda code, the dashboard frontend and Python dependencies at the edge. This reduces the risk of committing secrets or releasing vulnerable dependencies. This is a potential application of the principles, not a claim that the project uses CodePipeline or ECS.
7. Conclusion DevSecOps promotes accountable release workflows by automating repeatable checks, defining acceptance conditions and keeping deployments traceable.
References AWS CodePipeline Manual approval AWS CodeBuild AWS Security Hub AWS CloudTrail

title: Proposal
content:
Driver Drowsiness & Distraction Detection An Edge AI and AWS Serverless Solution for Driver Monitoring 1. Executive Summary This project proposes a prototype for detecting signs of driver drowsiness and distraction using Computer Vision, Edge AI and AWS Cloud. A webcam captures facial images, which are processed locally using OpenCV and MediaPipe Face Mesh with 478 facial landmarks. Eye Aspect Ratio (EAR), Mouth Aspect Ratio (MAR), head pose and experimental gaze direction are extracted to support temporal, rule-based analysis.
Instead of continuously uploading video, the device sends only event metadata to AWS. A serverless backend validates, stores and retrieves events, while an authenticated web dashboard allows authorized users to review event history. The design aims to reduce network usage and latency, preserve privacy and minimize infrastructure management. The prototype is an awareness and research tool, not a certified driver safety system.
2. Problem Statement Current problem Prolonged eye closure, yawning, changes in head orientation and changes in gaze may indicate drowsiness or distraction. These signs can be difficult to notice in time. Continuous cloud-based video processing requires bandwidth and may introduce latency, increase costs and expose sensitive facial data. Unstable connectivity can also interrupt event reporting.
Proposed solution The system separates local detection from cloud event management. The edge device extracts facial features and analyzes them over time. When a candidate event is detected, it generates an event_id and prepares metadata for local buffering and synchronization. An AWS HTTP API forwards the event to a Lambda writer, which validates the payload and uses a conditional DynamoDB write to prevent duplicate records. A separate Lambda reader serves authorized history queries. The dashboard uses Amazon Cognito for authentication and Amazon CloudFront with a private S3 origin for frontend delivery.
Benefits and return on investment Local video processing reduces reliance on network connectivity for detection and avoids uploading raw video. Centralized event history supports review and future analysis without maintaining a dedicated server. Serverless, usage-based infrastructure limits idle resource costs at prototype scale. Reusing a laptop and webcam, if available, avoids additional hardware expenditure. The anticipated value is technical and educational: a reusable Edge AI pipeline, a cloud integration reference and hands-on experience with AWS services. Financial savings, accident reduction and a monetary ROI have not been measured; no payback period is claimed.
3. Solution Architecture The proposed system consists of three layers: edge processing, cloud event management and an authenticated dashboard.
Figure 1. Overall architecture of the Driver Drowsiness & Distraction Detection system using Edge AI and AWS Cloud.
Data flow The webcam captures facial images locally. Raw video is not sent to AWS. OpenCV and MediaPipe Face Mesh extract 478 landmarks and calculate EAR, MAR, head pose and experimental gaze features. Temporal analysis uses rule-based candidates and CSV-based evaluation to distinguish sustained abnormal patterns from short movements. A detected event receives a unique event_id. The planned local event buffer retains unsynchronized metadata and retries when connectivity returns. The device sends an HTTPS POST /events request to Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API). The ingestion route must authenticate the device or its authorized identity before deployment. AWS Lambda Event Writer validates the payload and uses a DynamoDB conditional PutItem based on the unique event key. A repeated event must not create another record; an acknowledged duplicate should be treated as already synchronized. The dashboard signs users in through Amazon Cognito and obtains JWTs. API Gateway uses a JWT authorizer for protected routes. An authorized GET /events request invokes Lambda Event Reader, which queries DynamoDB and returns paginated event history. The backend must enforce ownership or authorized scope, not merely token validity. Amazon CloudFront delivers the static dashboard from a private Amazon S3 bucket using Origin Access Control (OAC). Amazon CloudWatch monitors API access logs, Lambda logs, errors, duration and DynamoDB metrics. AWS IAM, CloudTrail and AWS Budgets support permissions, auditing and spending oversight. AWS WAF is optional; if selected, its attachment point and coverage must be verified. AWS services used or planned Service Role Amazon API Gateway HTTP API for event ingestion and history retrieval; JWT authorization for protected routes AWS Lambda Separate Event Writer and Event Reader functions Amazon DynamoDB Event metadata storage, conditional writes and history queries Amazon Cognito User registration, sign-in and JWT issuance Amazon S3 Private storage for static dashboard files Amazon CloudFront HTTPS frontend delivery with OAC Amazon CloudWatch Logs, operational metrics and alarms AWS IAM Least-privilege permissions for AWS resources AWS CloudTrail Auditing AWS account activity AWS Budgets Budget tracking and spending alerts AWS WAF (optional) Additional web protection, subject to compatibility and budget Component and data design The edge pipeline runs independently of cloud connectivity. The proposed event schema includes event_id, device_id, event_type, UTC timestamp, duration and relevant derived features. Final field names, detection thresholds and retention periods will be defined during implementation. A proposed DynamoDB design uses event_id as a unique primary key and an authorized device/user scope plus timestamp as an index for history queries; the final index and access model must be validated against the actual query patterns.
The writer should reject malformed payloads, verify the identity and permitted device scope, and avoid storing raw images or video. The reader should restrict queries to the caller’s authorized scope. JWTs, credentials and sensitive payloads must not be exposed in source code or logs. The S3 bucket will block public access, with CloudFront OAC granted only the required origin access. Event metadata may still be sensitive, so access and retention need to be controlled.
4. Technical Implementation Implementation phases Edge AI and feature extraction: configure webcam capture, OpenCV and MediaPipe; calculate EAR, MAR and head pose; evaluate gaze as an experimental feature. Temporal analysis and reliability: analyze CSV feature data, calibrate rules and event durations, implement a persistent local event buffer and bounded retry with backoff; preserve event IDs across retries. Serverless backend: configure DynamoDB, Lambda Writer/Reader, API Gateway routes, request validation and conditional writes; verify authorized device ingestion and history retrieval. Dashboard and security: configure Cognito, JWT authorization and backend access checks; host the static frontend in private S3 and deliver through CloudFront OAC; configure IAM and monitoring. Validation and workshop: test detection, synchronization, duplicate delivery, access control and cloud integration; estimate costs, prepare demonstration evidence and document cleanup steps. Technical requirements Layer Requirements Edge device Computer with webcam, Python, OpenCV, MediaPipe and local storage Analysis EAR, MAR, head pose, experimental gaze, CSV evaluation and temporal rules Cloud AWS account, HTTP API, Lambda, DynamoDB, Cognito, S3 and CloudFront Operations IAM permissions, CloudWatch logging and alarms, CloudTrail and Budgets Testing Controlled lighting and head angles, sample labeled events, network interruption, duplicate requests and unauthorized requests Current implementation status According to the project self-assessment, the webcam-based edge pipeline and facial feature extraction have been developed. Gaze direction remains experimental and temporal rule-based analysis requires refinement. The AWS architecture has been designed; end-to-end cloud deployment and dashboard functionality have not yet been confirmed. The local buffer, retry mechanism, accuracy evaluation and network recovery tests remain to be completed. These are planned deliverables, not claims of completed validation.
5. Timeline & Milestones The following is a proposed schedule aligned with the existing Worklog dates and the intended submission at the end of Week 10. Activities should be recorded as completed only when actually performed.
Week Dates (2026) Planned activities and milestones 1–5 05 Oct – 06 Nov AWS foundations, networking, compute, storage, serverless and AI/ML study 6 09–13 Nov Analyze the problem, define scope, research Edge AI and design the architecture 7 16–20 Nov Develop facial feature extraction and evaluate EAR, MAR, head pose and experimental gaze 8 23–27 Nov Refine temporal analysis, local buffering and retry; implement the event ingestion backend 9 30 Nov – 04 Dec Implement protected history access, dashboard delivery, IAM and monitoring 10 07–11 Dec Test the prototype, finalize costs, document the workshop, prepare demo and submit the report Target submission: 11 December 2026, subject to FCAJ approval of the submission schedule and required internship duration.
6. Budget Estimation Planning assumptions The following assumptions are illustrative for a small prototype, not measured usage: one edge device, up to five test users, 10,000 event submissions and 10,000 history requests per month, 20,000 Lambda invocations at 128 MB and 200 ms average duration, 1 GB of DynamoDB data including indexes, 0.1 GB of S3 storage, 10,000 CloudFront HTTPS requests, 1 GB of frontend transfer, 0.5 GB of CloudWatch log ingestion and two standard alarms. Additional retries, index operations and history query pagination must be counted when estimating actual usage.
Infrastructure budget Service / cost category Estimated monthly usage Proposed budget allocation (USD/month) API Gateway and Lambda 20,000 API requests and invocations 0.50 DynamoDB On-demand reads/writes and 1 GB storage including indexes 1.00 Cognito Up to five test users; confirm selected tier 0.50 S3 and CloudFront Static hosting, requests and 1 GB transfer 1.00 CloudWatch Logs, storage and two alarms 1.00 CloudTrail, Budgets and miscellaneous charges Basic account auditing and budget notifications 0.50 Contingency Additional requests or data transfer 0.50 Total planning budget 5.00 This is a proposed spending allocation, not an AWS Pricing Calculator quotation or an actual bill. At the same monthly budget, a twelve-month planning ceiling would be USD 60; the workshop is only a short prototype. Hardware cost is assumed to be zero additional expenditure if the existing computer and webcam are reused. Paid WAF, SMS/MFA charges, optional backups, taxes and additional traffic are excluded and must be estimated separately if required.
Before submission, select the actual AWS Region, confirm service tiers and workload, create an estimate using the AWS Pricing Calculator and add its actual share link or exported PDF. Use AWS pricing to verify applicable rates and free-tier eligibility. Set budget alerts (for example, at 50%, 80% and 100% of the proposed USD 5 budget), limit log retention and remove unused resources. AWS Budgets alerts do not automatically cap spending.
7. Risk Assessment Risk matrix and mitigation Risk Likelihood Impact Proposed mitigation Poor lighting, occlusion or unusual head angles Medium High Evaluate under controlled variations; flag unreliable face tracking False positive or missed detection Medium High Calibrate thresholds, use temporal rules and measure performance on labeled samples Unstable network Medium Medium Persistent local buffering and retry with backoff Duplicate event submissions Medium Medium Stable event IDs and conditional DynamoDB writes Unauthorized access or sensitive data exposure Medium High Authenticated ingestion, JWT, ownership checks, IAM, private S3 and minimal metadata Unexpected AWS charges Low–Medium Medium Usage monitoring, budget alerts, limited retention and cleanup Schedule or integration delays Medium Medium Prioritize edge detection, ingestion, authorized history and demo; defer optional features Contingency plans When the network is unavailable, local detection should continue and unsynchronized metadata should remain buffered until connectivity returns. If a feature is unreliable, report the limitation and restrict its use to experimentation. If an optional cloud component cannot be completed within the schedule, document its status and demonstrate the verified core path. Tests should be conducted in a safe, stationary environment, not by intentionally inducing distraction or drowsiness while driving.
8. Expected Outcomes Technical deliverables and evaluation A local computer vision prototype that extracts facial features and identifies candidate events using temporal rules. A metadata-only event synchronization workflow with a local buffer, retry and duplicate handling. An authenticated AWS dashboard displaying event history through a serverless backend. Documented tests covering controlled facial movements, lighting/head angles, network recovery, duplicate requests and authorization. Report observed precision/recall or false-positive and missed-event counts if labeled data is sufficient; do not claim accuracy without measurements. Architecture diagram, bilingual workshop instructions, cost estimate, monitoring evidence, demo and resource cleanup instructions. Long-term value The project provides a reusable foundation for further Edge AI research, improvements to temporal analysis and scalable event-driven applications. Gaze analysis remains an experimental extension until validated. The prototype is intended to support awareness and research and must not be relied upon as a substitute for safe driving practices or a validated automotive safety product.

title: Blog 2
content:
Amazon S3: Storing, Protecting and Delivering Data on AWS 1. Amazon S3 overview Amazon S3 provides object storage for application files, documents, analytical datasets, backups and static website assets. Unlike a disk attached to a server, applications interact with objects through API operations.
2. Data structure A bucket is a container, an object is data with metadata, and an object key identifies the object within a bucket. For example, dashboard/assets/app.js identifies a JavaScript file. Slashes organize keys into prefixes without requiring physical directories.
3. Selecting a storage class Storage class Suitable workload S3 Standard Frequently accessed data S3 Intelligent-Tiering Changing access patterns S3 Standard-IA Infrequent access with fast retrieval S3 One Zone-IA Re-creatable data stored in one AZ S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval Long-term storage with fast retrieval S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval Archives that can tolerate restoration time S3 Glacier Deep Archive Very rarely accessed archives S3 Express One Zone Low-latency workloads using directory buckets Consider retrieval charges, minimum storage durations and recovery requirements before choosing a class.
4. Management and security Keep Block Public Access enabled for private buckets; grant only necessary IAM and bucket-policy permissions. Use server-side encryption and consider SSE-KMS for suitable key management and audit requirements. Use Versioning to help recover from accidental overwrites or deletions; manage older versions using Lifecycle. Configure Lifecycle transitions or expiration according to retention requirements. 5. Hands-on guide: secure frontend delivery Create a general purpose bucket in the selected Region and keep Block Public Access enabled. Upload HTML, CSS and JavaScript for a sample website and inspect the content types. Create a CloudFront distribution using an S3 REST origin (not the S3 website endpoint) and Origin Access Control (OAC). Update the bucket policy to allow the specified CloudFront distribution to read required objects. Set index.html as the default root object, use HTTPS and test the CloudFront domain. Verify that unauthorized direct object access is denied while CloudFront can deliver the content. Remove test resources when no longer needed. 6. Data and machine learning applications S3 can store datasets, model artifacts and analytical outputs. Organize data by prefixes, grant processing permissions separately and apply retention policies. Costs depend on capacity, requests, retrieval and data transfer.
7. Connection to the internship project In the Driver Drowsiness & Distraction Detection architecture, S3 holds dashboard frontend assets and CloudFront delivers them through OAC. Webcam video is not uploaded to S3; event metadata is stored in DynamoDB. This separation aligns with the project’s privacy and data-transfer goals.
8. Conclusion Effective S3 design identifies what is stored, who can read it, how long it remains and how it is accessed. A bucket should not be made public simply to simplify website deployment.

title: Blog 3
content:
Amazon EventBridge Scheduler: Automating Recurring Tasks with AWS Lambda 1. Why use a scheduling service? Applications often need periodic tasks such as report generation, data checks or notifications. Keeping a server running solely to wait for a task adds operational work. EventBridge Scheduler provides AWS-managed scheduling that invokes configured targets.
2. Schedule types Type Example Purpose Rate-based rate(30 minutes) Repeat at regular intervals Cron-based cron(0 8 * * ? *) Run daily at 08:00 in the configured time zone One-time at(2026-12-01T08:00:00) Run once at a specified time Scheduler supports time zones for cron and one-time schedules. Its scheduling precision is at the minute level, not suitable for second-level real-time control.
3. Components and reliability Reference flow: Schedule → Execution role → Lambda → CloudWatch Logs.
The execution role authorizes Scheduler to invoke a specific target. A retry policy defines retry limits and the maximum age of undelivered events. An Amazon SQS dead-letter queue (DLQ) can capture events that could not be delivered after the retry conditions are exhausted. A flexible time window is useful when invocation can occur within an interval rather than at a fixed minute.
Scheduler provides at-least-once delivery, so business logic should be idempotent when duplicate executions could cause side effects.
4. Hands-on guide: invoke Lambda every 30 minutes Create a Lambda function with a supported Python runtime and a simple handler:
import json from datetime import datetime, timezone def lambda_handler(event, context): result = { "task": "scheduled-check", "timestamp": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat() } print(json.dumps(result)) return result In the Lambda console, create scheduled-check and grant CloudWatch Logs permissions. Open EventBridge Scheduler, select Create schedule and name it check-every-30-minutes. Select a recurring rate-based schedule, enter rate(30 minutes) and turn the flexible time window off if a fixed schedule is required. Select AWS Lambda as the target, choose the function and configure an execution role with lambda:InvokeFunction permission for that function. Configure a suitable retry policy, optionally add an SQS DLQ, enable the schedule and save. Inspect the Lambda logs in CloudWatch after invocation. Delete the schedule, function and dedicated lab resources when no longer required. 5. Validation scenarios Scenario Expected result Enabled schedule and valid permissions Target receives scheduled invocations Missing Lambda invocation permission Scheduler records a delivery error Retries exhausted with a configured DLQ Undelivered event reaches the DLQ if authorized Duplicate Lambda event Business logic avoids duplicate side effects Function execution failures after an asynchronous request has been accepted by Lambda require separate monitoring and handling at the Lambda layer.
6. Connection to the internship project Scheduler could aggregate daily drowsiness and distraction event counts or generate periodic reports from DynamoDB metadata. This is a possible extension for Driver Drowsiness & Distraction Detection, not a replacement for immediate edge alerts or a required component of the current architecture.
7. Conclusion EventBridge Scheduler is suitable for background tasks with clear timing requirements. Restricting permissions, handling duplicates, monitoring failures and deleting unused schedules improve operational reliability.

title: Access S3 from on-premises
content:
Overview In this section, you will create an Interface endpoint to access Amazon S3 from a simulated on-premises environment. The Interface endpoint will allow you to route to Amazon S3 over a VPN connection from your simulated on-premises environment.
Why using Interface endpoint:
Gateway endpoints only work with resources running in the VPC where they are created. Interface endpoints work with resources running in VPC, and also resources running in on-premises environments. Connectivty from your on-premises environment to the cloud can be provided by AWS Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Interface endpoints allow you to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink. These services include some AWS services, services hosted by other AWS customers and partners in their own VPCs (referred to as PrivateLink Endpoint Services), and supported AWS Marketplace Partner services. For this workshop, we will focus on connecting to Amazon S3.

title: On-premises DNS Simulation
content:
AWS PrivateLink endpoints have a fixed IP address in each Availability Zone where they are deployed, for the life of the endpoint (until it is deleted). These IP addresses are attached to Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). AWS recommends using DNS to resolve the IP addresses for endpoints so that downstream applications use the latest IP addresses when ENIs are added to new AZs, or deleted over time.
In this section, you will create a forwarding rule to send DNS resolution requests from a simulated on-premises environment to a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone. This section leverages the infrastructure deployed by CloudFormation in the Prepare the environment section.
Create DNS Alias Records for the Interface endpoint Navigate to the Route 53 management console (Hosted Zones section). The CloudFormation template you deployed in the Prepare the environment section created this Private Hosted Zone. Click on the name of the Private Hosted Zone, s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com: Create a new record in the Private Hosted Zone: Record name and record type keep default options Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor (you saved when doing section 4.3) Click Add another record, and add a second record using the following values. Click Create records when finished to create both records. Record name: *. Record type: keep default value (type A) Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor The new records appear in the Route 53 console:
Create a Resolver Forwarding Rule Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rules allow you to forward DNS queries from your VPC to other sources for name resolution. Outside of a workshop environment, you might use this feature to forward DNS queries from your VPC to DNS servers running on-premises. In this section, you will simulate an on-premises conditional forwarder by creating a forwarding rule that forwards DNS queries for Amazon S3 to a Private Hosted Zone running in “VPC Cloud” in-order to resolve the PrivateLink interface endpoint regional DNS name.
From the Route 53 management console, click Inbound endpoints on the left side bar In the Inbound endpoints console, click the ID of the inbound endpoint Copy the two IP addresses listed to your text editor From the Route 53 menu, choose Resolver > Rules, and click Create rule: In the Create rule console: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: VPC On-prem Outbound endpoint: VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint Target IP Addresses: Enter both IP addresses from your text editor (inbound endpoint addresses) and then click Submit You have successfully created resolver forwarding rule.
Test the on-premises DNS Simulation Connect to Test-Interface-Endpoint EC2 instance with Session manager Test DNS resolution. The dig command will return the IP addresses assigned to the VPC Interface endpoint running in VPC Cloud (your IP’s will be different): dig +short s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com The IP addresses returned are the VPC endpoint IP addresses, NOT the Resolver IP addresses you pasted from your text editor. The IP addresses of the Resolver endpoint and the VPC endpoint look similar because they are all from the VPC Cloud CIDR block.
Navigate to the VPC menu (Endpoints section), select the S3 Interface endpoint. Click the Subnets tab and verify that the IP addresses returned by Dig match the VPC endpoint: Return to your shell and use the AWS CLI to test listing your S3 buckets: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Terminate your Session Manager session: In this section you created an Interface endpoint for Amazon S3. This endpoint can be reached from on-premises through Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints simulated forwarding DNS requests from on-premises to a Private Hosted Zone running the cloud. Route 53 inbound Endpoints recieved the resolution request and returned a response containing the IP addresses of the VPC interface endpoint. Using DNS to resolve the endpoint IP addresses provides high availability in-case of an Availability Zone outage.

title: VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
When you create an interface or gateway endpoint, you can attach an endpoint policy to it that controls access to the service to which you are connecting. A VPC endpoint policy is an IAM resource policy that you attach to an endpoint. If you do not attach a policy when you create an endpoint, AWS attaches a default policy for you that allows full access to the service through the endpoint.
You can create a policy that restricts access to specific S3 buckets only. This is useful if you only want certain S3 Buckets to be accessible through the endpoint.
In this section you will create a VPC endpoint policy that restricts access to the S3 bucket specified in the VPC endpoint policy.
Connect to an EC2 instance and verify connectivity to S3 Start a new AWS Session Manager session on the instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. From the session, verify that you can list the contents of the bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC: aws s3 ls s3://\<your-bucket-name\> The bucket contents include the two 1 GB files uploaded in earlier.
Create a new S3 bucket; follow the naming pattern you used in Part 1, but add a ‘-2’ to the name. Leave other fields as default and click create Successfully create bucket
Navigate to: Services > VPC > Endpoints, then select the Gateway VPC endpoint you created earlier. Click the Policy tab. Click Edit policy. The default policy allows access to all S3 Buckets through the VPC endpoint.
In Edit Policy console, copy & Paste the following policy, then replace yourbucketname-2 with your 2nd bucket name. This policy will allow access through the VPC endpoint to your new bucket, but not any other bucket in Amazon S3. Click Save to apply the policy. { "Id": "Policy1631305502445", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Stmt1631305501021", "Action": "s3:*", "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2", "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2/*" ], "Principal": "*" } ] } Successfully customize policy
From your session on the Test-Gateway-Endpoint instance, test access to the S3 bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC aws s3 ls s3://<yourbucketname> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy:
Return to your home directory on your EC2 instance cd~ Create a file fallocate -l 1G test-bucket2.xyz Copy file to 2nd bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-2nd-bucket-name> This operation succeeds because it is permitted by the VPC endpoint policy.
Then we test access to the first bucket by copy the file to 1st bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-1st-bucket-name> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy.
Part 3 Summary: In this section, you created a VPC endpoint policy for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to test the policy. AWS CLI actions targeted to your original S3 bucket failed because you applied a policy that only allowed access to the second bucket you created. AWS CLI actions targeted for your second bucket succeeded because the policy allowed them. These policies can be useful in situations where you need to control access to resources through VPC endpoints.
